summary.text: An island arc is a long chain of active volcanoes with intense earthquake activity, found where two tectonic plates converge.
Most arcs start on oceanic crust as one plate's lithosphere sinks into the mantle at a subduction zone, and they are the main way continents grow.
Water released from the sinking slab lowers the mantle's melting temperature, and this is now thought to be the main driver of melting beneath arcs.

facts.label: Typical shape
facts.value: A distinct curve, with a deep trench alongside

facts.label: Where most are
facts.value: Near continents, especially the north and west Pacific

facts.label: Main water carrier
facts.value: The mineral serpentinite in the sinking slab

facts.label: Basin behind the arc
facts.value: Back-arc basin, also called a marginal sea

items.prompt: Salt sprinkled on an icy road makes ice melt at a lower temperature. What does a similar job for the rock deep beneath an island arc?

options.label: Friction heat from the plates rubbing
Sunlight warming the shallow sea
Water released from the sinking plate
Salt carried down from the seafloor

items.explain: Water given off by the sinking slab lowers the mantle's melting temperature; the more water, the lower it drops.

items.prompt: Two ocean plates, one young and one much older, push into each other. Which one usually dives beneath the other?

options.label: The older plate
The younger plate
Whichever moves faster
Neither; both crumple upward

items.explain: Where two oceanic plates converge, the older plate subducts under the younger one.

items.prompt: Seismologists map earthquakes under an island arc, starting at the trench and moving toward the volcanoes. How do the quake depths change?

options.label: They stay at the same shallow depth
They get shallower toward the arc
They jump around with no pattern
They get deeper beneath the arc

items.explain: Quakes along the subduction boundary sit at increasing depth under the arc, tracing the sinking plate; this band is the Benioff zone.

items.prompt: What pulls the seafloor down to make the deep, narrow trench beside an island arc?

options.label: The weight of the volcanoes on the arc
Gravity tugging on the dense sinking plate
Strong currents scouring the ocean floor
Magma chambers collapsing beneath the sea

items.explain: The trench forms from the downward gravitational pull of the relatively dense subducting plate on its leading edge.

items.prompt: Scientists once thought friction at the top of the sinking slab supplied the heat for melting. Why is that unlikely?

options.label: Hot mantle gets too runny for friction to melt it
The slab moves far too slowly to rub at all
The ocean above cools the slab completely
Friction only happens close to the surface

items.explain: At the temperatures needed to melt, the asthenosphere's viscosity would be so low that shear melting could not happen.

items.prompt: The Mariana Trench is the deepest trench in any ocean basin. About how deep is it?

options.label: About 1,100 m
About 4,000 m
About 11,000 m
About 110,000 m

items.explain: The Mariana Trench reaches roughly 11,000 m (36,000 ft), deeper than any other ocean feature.

paragraphs.heading: Volcano chains at plate edges
paragraphs.text: An island arc is a long chain of active volcanoes with strong earthquake activity. Arcs sit along convergent tectonic plate boundaries. Most begin on ocean crust, formed as lithosphere sinks down into the mantle along a subduction zone. Island arcs are the main way continents grow.

paragraphs.heading: Active and inactive arcs
paragraphs.text: An arc counts as active or inactive depending on its earthquakes and whether it has volcanoes. An active arc is a ridge of recent volcanoes with a deep earthquake zone beneath it. It has a clear curved shape and a trench in the deep sea. On its outer, convex side there is also a big negative Bouguer anomaly. An inactive arc is a chain of islands made of older volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks.

paragraphs.heading: Trench and Benioff zone
paragraphs.text: On the side where one plate dives down lies a deep, narrow ocean trench. It marks the line at the surface where the sinking plate meets the plate on top. The pull of gravity on the dense, sinking plate drags its front edge down and creates the trench. Earthquakes along this boundary happen deeper and deeper beneath the arc, and together they trace a plane dipping under the upper plate, called the Benioff zone.

paragraphs.heading: Why the mantle melts
paragraphs.text: Where the heat comes from to melt the mantle was long disputed. Friction at the top of the sinking slab was once the favoured answer, but hot asthenosphere becomes too runny for that kind of melting to happen. Scientists now think water is the main driver. The more water a sinking slab carries, the lower the temperature at which the mantle melts. As pressure rises, minerals in the slab change form and release that water, and serpentinite is the mineral that carries the most.

paragraphs.heading: Mantle flow and wet melting
paragraphs.text: Heat from the surrounding asthenosphere flows into the sinking slab, leaving the nearby asthenosphere cooler and stiffer. That stiffer layer is dragged down with the slab, and softer mantle flows in behind it. When this sinking mantle meets watery fluids rising from the slab, it is thought to begin partly melting. Some melt may also come from hot mantle rising so fast that the drop in pressure alone makes it melt.

paragraphs.heading: The parts of an arc
paragraphs.text: Most arcs share a common layout. The fore-arc holds the trench, the accretionary prism and a fore-arc basin where flat layers of sediment settle undisturbed. Trenches form on the ocean side of arcs and are the deepest places in ocean basins; the Mariana Trench reaches about 11,000 m. On the inner, concave side lies a back-arc basin, or marginal sea, which opens when an existing arc is pulled apart by rifting.

paragraphs.heading: Where arcs are found
paragraphs.text: Most modern island arcs lie close to the edges of continents, especially along the northern and western rim of the Pacific. They also form where two ocean plates meet, and then the older plate sinks beneath the younger one. Evidence from some continental margins hints that in late Mesozoic or early Cenozoic times, certain arcs may have moved closer to the continents. Even so, nothing inside the arcs themselves proves they have always been where they are now.
